c1.story:
This is the industry of the notebook in your child's school bag, the carton your toothpaste came in, the plywood inside your wardrobe and the glossy laminate on your kitchen cabinets. It is also, if we are honest, one of the messier buckets in the market, because it groups together businesses that share a raw material, wood, and very little else.

Door one is the paper and board mill. JK Paper at Rayagada in Odisha and Songadh in Gujarat, West Coast Paper at Dandeli in Karnataka, Trident's straw-based mill in Punjab. They pulp eucalyptus, subabul, bamboo or wheat straw and turn it into writing paper and packaging board, sold by the tonne. The trouble is that a tonne of copier paper from Indonesia is, to most buyers, the same as a tonne from Odisha, so imports set the price.

Door two is the branded panel and surface maker: Century Plyboards, Greenply, Greenpanel, Greenlam. They make plywood, MDF, particle board and laminates and sell them through dealers to carpenters. And here is the interesting bit: the customer who picks the brand is often not the homeowner but the carpenter, who trusts a name, knows how it cuts and does not want callbacks. A brand that wins carpenters can hold its price when unbranded rivals cannot.

Door three is the packaging converter, TCPL Packaging with its printed cartons, AGI Greenpac with its glass bottles. It buys board or glass and turns it into packaging for FMCG, liquor and pharma brands under contract.

Door four is an honest admission: Welspun Corp makes steel pipes, Vardhman and Sanathan make yarn, Jain Resource Recycling recycles metal. Our data source files them here, but they belong to other cycles.

Same tree, three different businesses: one sells weight, one sells trust, and one sells to a brand.
c1.read:
Four tiles. Read each top to bottom, then compare the profit bars across the row.

  • The line under the name tells you how the product is sold. Paper by the tonne at an import-set price. Panels and laminates through dealers and carpenters. Packaging under contract to big brands. And a fourth tile that explicitly says these companies run on their own cycles.
  • The tickers open each stock's page. The tiles are approximate: STYLAMIND, for instance, sits on the converters tile, though by product it is a laminate maker, close in spirit to door two. TRIDENT appears under paper because of its straw-based mill, but most of its business is towels and yarn.
  • The profit bar is the key comparison. Paper mills show low: they cannot set their price when imports flood in. Panels show medium: the brand and the carpenter relationship give some pricing power. Converters show medium: they pass input costs on to big customers, but those customers are powerful enough to keep the margin in check. The fourth tile shows low, mostly as a warning not to read those names through this industry's lens.
  • The bet line is what you are really buying: a paper price against wood cost, home interiors and brand grip, or consumer volumes.

Before going further, put every name you own on a tile. If it is on the fourth, go to its real industry's explainer instead: Welspun Corp with steel pipes, Vardhman with textiles, Jain with metals. Everything else on this page is about the first three tiles.

c2.story:
India has a peculiar problem for a paper and wood industry: it does not grow much commercial timber. Natural forests are protected, as they should be, and cutting forest wood for industry is tightly restricted. So station one of this kitchen is a farm.

Over the past few decades, paper mills have built networks of farm forestry contracts. They hand out high-yield eucalyptus and subabul saplings to farmers in Andhra Pradesh, Telangana, Odisha, Gujarat and Karnataka, help them plant, and promise to buy the wood a few years later. It is a clever system, but it has a weakness: the farmer can always switch crops. If cotton or chilli pays better, he plants that instead, and a few years later the mill finds wood scarce and expensive. Panel makers cluster in Uttarakhand, Punjab and the North-East for similar reasons, close to plantation timber like poplar. Imported pulp, imported timber and waste paper collected from cities complete station one.

Station two is pulping and pressing: wood is cooked into pulp in a mill, or peeled into veneer and pressed into boards. Station three is the paper machine and the board line, giant machines that turn pulp into a continuous sheet, or fibre into MDF. This is precisely where imports compete head on. Indonesian giants like Asia Pulp and Paper and APRIL make paper at enormous scale next to their own plantations, and under the ASEAN trade agreement it arrives at low duty.

Station four is converting and finishing: board printed into cartons, laminates pressed, panels cut and branded. Station five is the customer: schools, offices, publishers, FMCG brands, carpenters and furniture makers.

The squeeze, then, is clear. Wood is expensive at station one, and imports cap the price at station three. A mill caught between the two has nowhere to go.
c2.read:
Read the diagram in two passes: the station boxes left to right, then the band rows below.

The five boxes go from fibre to buyer. Under each name you see what happens and who does it. Notice that the same listed names, JKPAPER, WSTCSTPAPR, GREENPANEL, CENTURYPLY and GREENPLY, appear at stations two and three: these are integrated businesses running pulp and paper, or veneer and board, under one roof. The converters, TCPLPACK, AGI and GREENLAM, appear at station four.

The first band row is unusual. Station one reads farm forestry and imports. Station two reads India listed. Station three, the paper machines and board lines, is marked Asian imports, as a rival. Station four is India listed again, and station five is brands and carpenters. In other words, the band row shows Indian listed companies holding stations two and four, with the import threat sitting right between them at three. That is the visual version of the industry's problem.

The second band row shows where the rival stands, as the label says: Indonesia and China for paper and pulp, Southeast Asia for MDF and laminates. It spans the producing stations, with World under the buyers.

The note under the diagram explains the geography: little commercial timber, so mills contract farmers near Andhra, Odisha, Gujarat and Karnataka, and wood is the biggest cost. The so-what line is the key to reading any news: when imported paper or boards get cheap at station three, Indian mills cannot pass on their wood cost from station one, so the import price is the real lid on margins.

c3.story:
Paper, panels and packaging serve very different customers, and that is the most useful thing to understand about this industry's demand.

Paper follows education and paperwork. Writing and printing paper goes into notebooks, textbooks and exam papers, so demand rises with school enrolment, state textbook orders and the exam calendar. In 2020, when the pandemic shut schools and offices, writing paper demand collapsed almost overnight. Copier paper follows white-collar offices, and it is shrinking slowly as more of life moves to screens. Nobody expects a notebook boom; mills look for growth elsewhere.

That elsewhere is packaging. FMCG brands buy printed cartons and folding boxes for soaps, biscuits and medicines. E-commerce runs on corrugated boxes. Liquor and pharma companies buy glass bottles and blister board. Here a quiet policy tailwind matters: India's ban on several single-use plastic items in 2022 and the rules that make brands responsible for their packaging waste push companies towards paper and board.

Panels follow homes, and with a delay that is easy to miss. When a family buys a flat, it gets possession two or three years later, and only then does it call the carpenter to build wardrobes, kitchens and beds. So the strong housing sales of the past few years are turning into plywood, MDF and laminate demand now, as those flats are handed over. Offices, hotels and shops being fitted out add a second, smaller layer.

A flat sold today becomes a wardrobe order in two or three years. Panel makers live on that delay.

This is why the three doors can be in different moods at the same time: paper waiting for imports to ease, packaging steady with consumer volumes, panels warming up as completions arrive.
c3.read:
Each tile is a customer group: who buys, what they buy and what moves them. Sort them by door and the grid becomes a map.

  • Paper's tiles: education and publishing, which moves with enrolment, textbook orders and the exam season; and offices, which moves with white-collar hiring and is slowly shrinking with digitisation.
  • Packaging's tiles: FMCG and food brands, moving with consumer volumes and plastic bans; e-commerce and logistics, moving with online orders and the festive season; and liquor and pharma, moving with liquor volumes and pharma exports.
  • Panels' tiles: home interiors and furniture, moving with housing completions, renovation and the real-estate cycle; and commercial real estate, moving with office leasing and hotel building.

Look at the third lines. The word completions on the home interiors tile is the most important word on this card for panel investors. It is not housing sales or launches; it is the moment the keys are handed over. That is why the so-what line calls recent real-estate strength a delayed tailwind for panels.

Also notice the one tile with a structural headwind: offices, where digitisation is a slow drain. And the one with a structural tailwind: FMCG brands, helped by plastic bans.

To use the grid, map each company you own. A writing paper mill sits mostly on the first two tiles, which is why its growth is limited. A board maker leans on packaging. A panel brand sits almost entirely on the last two, which makes it a delayed bet on housing.

c4.story:
A paper mill and a panel maker both buy wood, but they make money in different ways, and the difference shows up in how steady their profits are.

For a paper mill, wood, pulp and chemicals are the biggest bill, followed closely by power, steam, people and freight. A paper machine is a power-hungry beast, and most mills run their own captive power plants burning coal and biomass, often including the bark and black liquor from their own process. The selling price, though, is set by imports. When Indonesian copier paper lands cheap, the mill must match it, whatever its wood cost. Since 2022 Indian wood prices have stayed stubbornly high, as farmers found other crops more rewarding, and that combination of dear wood and cheap imports is why paper margins have been squeezed.

A panel maker spends a bigger share on wood and resins, but its pricing is stickier, thanks to the brand. The carpenter who asks for a particular plywood brand is not going to switch for a small discount. That stickiness costs money, though: advertising, dealer schemes and loyalty programmes for carpenters are a real line in a panel maker's accounts, the price of the brand premium.

Then there is the line that explains today's thin panel margins: capex. In 2023 and 2024, almost every panel maker added new MDF lines at the same time, betting on the housing boom and on MDF replacing plywood in modular furniture. Each line was a sensible decision. Together they flooded the market, utilisation fell and discounting began.

Every panel maker made the right call on MDF demand. They just all made it at once.

Depreciation and interest jumped for the builders before the lines filled, and the payback depends on how fast utilisation climbs back.
c4.read:
Two charts walk one hundred rupees of sales down to what is left: paper and board mills, then wood panels and surfaces. Read each left to right.

  • The input bar is wood, pulp and chemicals. It takes a little under half of a paper mill's sales and a little over half of a panel maker's. Paper mills that grow their own fibre through farm forestry spend less here than a panel maker buying timber, veneer and resin.
  • The opex bar is power, people and freight. The paper mill's bar is notably taller, about a third of sales, because paper machines eat steam and electricity.
  • The depreciation and interest bar is bigger for paper mills, since a paper machine is a heavier asset than a plywood press.
  • The last bar is what is left, and here is a subtlety worth pausing on. In these mid-cycle shapes, the paper mill keeps a slightly larger slice than the panel maker. That does not contradict the profit bars on card one. The paper slice is the one that swings: in a boom it balloons, and when imports flood in it can almost vanish. The panel slice is thinner but steadier, because the brand holds price.

These are illustrative shapes, not any company's accounts; hover a bar for the rupee amount.

Below the charts, the list marks what matters. Realisation, wood cost and capex all get a yes; capex because of the MDF wave. Power, depreciation, working capital, interest and advertising are sometimes. Advertising is the one to watch at panel and laminate brands: a rising ad spend in a weak market is a brand defending its premium, which is usually a sign of strength.

c5.story:
Paper and panels went through the same cycle at the same time, but for slightly different reasons, and they may come out of it at different speeds.

In 2019 things were steady. Paper demand was fine, and panel makers were busy winning customers from the unorganised sector after the goods and services tax pushed some small players into the formal economy. Then 2020 hit: schools and offices shut, and writing paper demand collapsed for a year, even as packaging held up.

The boom of 2021 and 2022 was spectacular for paper. Schools reopened, global pulp prices spiked, shipping was chaotic and imports dried up. Indian mills suddenly had the domestic market to themselves and posted record margins. Panels boomed too, as people stuck at home decided to redo their kitchens and bedrooms.

The peak came around FY23. Paper realisations topped out, wood prices began to climb, and every panel maker announced new MDF capacity.

Then the long bust from 2023. Pulp prices fell, and Indonesian and Chinese paper flooded back in at prices Indian mills could not match while paying high wood costs. Paper stocks roughly halved from their peaks. In panels, the new MDF lines arrived together, and price wars broke out.

Now the clock says bottoming. Quality control orders on plywood, MDF and particle board came into force in 2025, blocking some low-grade imports. Housing completions are strong, and the new MDF lines are filling. Paper is still waiting: imports remain heavy, and the industry is asking for safeguard action. That is why the call prefers panels over paper: they share a clock, but panels are closer to the next hour.
c5.read:
Three pieces work together: the clock, the timeline and the four hands.

The clock has four arcs running clockwise from the top: boom, peak, bust and bottom. The labels under each arc date the last cycle: boom in 2021 and 2022, peak in FY23, bust from 2023 into 2025, bottom across 2025 and 2026. The long bust label is telling: this downturn dragged on for longer than the boom lasted. The arrow points to today, in the middle of the bottom arc, around half past ten. Not yet at the top of the dial, where an up-cycle begins. Hover an arc to read what defined it.

The timeline tells the story year by year, coloured by tone. A neutral 2019, the pandemic bust, the boom, the bust of 2023 and 2024, a neutral 2025 when the quality rules arrived, and the latest entry marked now. That last entry names the drivers of the bottom: housing completions, filling MDF lines, the request for safeguard action on paper imports, and plastic bans.

The four hands let you move the arrow yourself.

  • Imported paper landed price: low, arrow down. This is the hand paper mills are waiting on.
  • Domestic wood price: high but easing, a diamond. Falling wood is the fastest margin repair for both paper and panels.
  • MDF utilisation: rising, arrow up. The meaning line gives the thresholds: above three-quarters ends discounting, below two-thirds keeps the price war going.
  • Housing completions: strong, arrow up.

Notice which hands are green: the two that matter for panels. The one that matters most for paper is red.

c6.story:
What decides whether JK Paper or Century Plyboards has a good year? Three big dials, each with three dots of weight.

The first is the price of imported paper from Asia. It is the ceiling on Indian paper realisations. When Indonesian and Chinese mills are busy at home or global pulp is expensive, imports get dearer and Indian mills can raise prices. When Asian mills have spare capacity, they ship it to India under low ASEAN duties and Indian prices fall to match.

The second is the domestic wood price, the biggest input for paper and panels alike. It rises when farmers switch away from eucalyptus and poplar to better-paying crops, and because a tree takes years to grow, a wood shortage cannot be fixed quickly. High wood prices since 2022 have been the industry's persistent headache.

The third is housing activity, which drives panel and laminate demand with a lag. A strong property market today is a strong panel market as those homes are completed.

The two-dot dials are the global pulp price, which helps integrated mills by lifting import prices, and consumer volumes, which drive cartons for FMCG and pharma brands.

Then the smaller dials. The rupee is mixed: a weaker rupee makes imported pulp and chemicals dearer but also makes competing imports dearer, on balance a help to domestic mills. Coal and power costs matter for the captive power plants of paper mills. Interest rates matter for home loans and renovation. And plastic bans, a one-dot dial today, are a slow structural nudge from plastic towards paper that could grow in importance as packaging waste rules tighten.
c6.read:
Each row is one dial. Read across: the dial, the channel, what a rise does, and the weight in dots.

  • Three-dot rows: Asian paper import prices, domestic wood prices and housing activity. Start here. Note that the first two point in opposite directions: a rise in import prices helps the industry, a rise in wood prices hurts it. Their gap is the paper spread.
  • Arrows: green for import prices, housing, pulp, consumer volumes, plastic bans and consumer non-durables output. Red for wood, coal and power, and interest rates. A diamond for the rupee, which cuts both ways.
  • Channel tells you which door each dial reaches. Import prices and pulp reach paper mills. Housing and interest rates reach panels. Consumer volumes and plastic bans reach packaging. Wood reaches everyone.

The latest column shows a live reading where a dial maps to a series we track. Here several key dials have no live series: import prices, wood prices and pulp show a dash, because there is no clean public feed for them; follow them through company commentary and trade press. Housing uses the Nifty Realty index as a proxy, consumer volumes the Nifty FMCG index, and power costs the core-sector coal index. Treat proxies as a direction check rather than a measurement.

The quickest use of the table: check the two three-dot dials the so-what line names, imports and wood. If imports are getting dearer and wood is getting cheaper at the same time, paper margins are about to widen sharply. Today wood is easing but imports are not.

c7.story:
Why doesn't India, with a huge and growing appetite for paper, packaging and furniture, have a world-beating paper and wood industry? Two structural problems and a handful of cyclical ones explain it.

The first is wood itself. India's natural forests are protected, plantation wood depends on farmers' willingness to grow trees rather than crops, and a eucalyptus tree takes several years to be ready. When wood gets scarce, there is no quick fix. Indonesian and Brazilian producers, by contrast, run vast plantations of their own right next to their mills.

The second is imports. Asian mills are bigger, cheaper and plantation-integrated, and the ASEAN free trade agreement lets their paper in at low duty. As long as they have spare capacity, Indian mills face a lid on prices.

Then the cyclical bottleneck that caused the latest panel slump: capacity added in step. When every MDF maker expands at once, utilisation falls together and discounting follows. This is not a permanent problem, but it takes a couple of years to work through.

The slow-moving issues are the unorganised sector and digitisation. Thousands of small plywood and paper makers avoid taxes and skimp on standards, undercutting brands on price, though each year the formal economy squeezes them a little more. And offices and publishers use less paper every year, so growth must come from packaging.

Paper mills are also heavy water users and polluters, and state pollution boards can fine or shut them. And quality rules on imports are two-sided: BIS standards on panels can block cheap imports, but enforcement shifts and some supply finds a way around.
c7.read:
Each row is a bottleneck, with why it bites and a severity label. The label tells you how to treat each risk.

  • Structural: wood scarcity and cheap Asian imports. These are the two rows that cap returns for the whole industry. They show up in why Indian paper mills trade at modest multiples even in good years.
  • Slow: unorganised competition and digitisation. Both move over years. Unorganised competition is slowly fading as tax enforcement and quality rules bite, which is a tailwind for brands. Digitisation is slowly eroding writing paper, a headwind that pushes mills towards board and packaging.
  • Cyclical: capacity added in step. This is the row behind today's panel margins, and the one most likely to improve in the next couple of years as MDF lines fill.
  • Recurring: pollution rules. A paper mill closure order or a heavy fine is the kind of headline worth a news alert for each mill you own.
  • Two-sided: quality rules on imports. They help when enforced and leak when not.

Read the table as a story with a beginning and a middle. The first two rows are the permanent ceiling. The capacity row is the cyclical problem that is now healing, which is why the clock says bottoming. The quality rules row is the policy hinge: tighter enforcement, or a paper safeguard duty from the rulebook card, could move margins faster than any demand trend.

c8.story:
Few industries are as shaped by rules about trees, trade and plastic as this one.

Start with trees. The environment ministry and forest rules restrict cutting forest wood and govern plantations and the transit permits needed to move timber. That is a good thing for India's forests, but it is the reason wood supply depends on farm forestry and why wood prices are so sensitive to farmers' crop choices.

Then trade. The ASEAN free trade agreement, in force since 2010, lets paper from Indonesia and others in at low duty, which is the single biggest reason cheap imports keep arriving. The industry's hope sits in the trade remedies directorate, DGTR, which investigates dumping and import surges. An anti-dumping or safeguard duty on paper and board would lift paper realisations almost immediately, which is why the industry has been asking for one.

For panels, the big new rule is quality. The standards bureau's quality control orders on plywood, MDF and particle board, which came into force in 2025, make every panel sold in India, imported or local, meet a standard. That blocks some low-grade imports and squeezes unbranded local players who cut corners, putting a floor under quality and price for the brands.

And then plastic. The single-use plastic ban of 2022 and the rules making brands responsible for collecting their packaging waste push companies towards paper-based packaging. It is a slow tailwind, but a persistent one. Add the pollution boards, which can close a mill that fails effluent norms, and GST, whose rates shift demand between organised and unorganised players, and you have the full rulebook.
c8.read:
Each row is a regulator or rule. Read across: who it is, what it does, why you care, and its status. The status column is how to prioritise.

  • Always: the environment ministry and forest rules, the ASEAN free trade agreement, the pollution boards and GST. Permanent background. The ASEAN row deserves a second look: it is the rule behind the cheap-imports bottleneck on card seven.
  • Live: the single-use plastic ban and packaging waste rules. Actively shifting demand towards paper and board today.
  • New: the BIS quality control orders on plywood, MDF and particle board. This is the rule behind the panels' improving outlook. It matters most for branded panel makers.
  • Coming: DGTR and possible duties on paper. This is the single row that could change the paper story fastest. If a duty arrives, the import price ceiling lifts immediately, which is why it is the first item in the call's what-would-change list.

A useful habit: tick the rows that touch each company you own. A paper mill touches forest rules, ASEAN, DGTR, pollution boards and plastic rules. A panel brand touches forest rules, the quality orders and GST. A packaging converter touches the plastic rules most. The paper mill's longer list is another way of seeing why its profit bar on card one reads low.

Dated regulatory news for this industry, filtered from our feed, sits on the Picks and signals tab.

c9.story:
Porter's five forces boils down to one question: who gets to keep the money? Run the paper mills and the panel brands through it and you get two very different answers.

Paper mills face pressure from nearly every side. Rivalry is fierce: Indian mills compete with each other and, more painfully, with Asian imports, on a product that is hard to tell apart. Suppliers have more power than you might expect: there are many farmers and timber sellers, but wood is scarce, so prices rise, and imported pulp is priced globally. Buyers switch on price; a school-notebook maker buys whichever paper is cheapest this month. Substitutes are real: every email, e-book and digital form is a page of paper not printed. Only new entrants offer some relief, because building a paper mill takes huge capital and years.

The panel, surface and packaging group does noticeably better, and the reason is the buyer. Carpenters and homeowners are loyal to brands. A carpenter who has used a particular plywood for years trusts it to cut cleanly and not warp, and his reputation depends on it. That loyalty is the moat, and it is why panel brands spend so much on dealer schemes and carpenter programmes: they are paying to maintain the buyer spoke.

But the panel group has one weakness the paper mills do not: new entrants. Setting up a plywood unit or a carton-printing line is cheap, which is why unorganised players abound. The brands keep winning share, but they never get the market to themselves.
c9.read:
The radar has five spokes, one per force. The further a shape reaches along a spoke, the more pressure on the business, so a smaller shape is the better business.

Two shapes: paper and board mills, and panels, surfaces and packaging. Look at overall size first. The paper shape is bigger almost everywhere. Its rivalry spoke reaches the full three, its supplier and buyer spokes reach two and a half, and substitutes reach two.

The biggest single gap is on the buyer spoke: two and a half for paper against one and a half for panels and packaging. That one spoke is the brand advantage in a picture.

Then look for where the shapes cross. On new entrants, the panels group reaches further than paper, two against one and a half. That is the unorganised plywood and converting sector: easy to enter, hard to eliminate. It is the panel brands' permanent irritant.

The table beside the chart gives each score from zero to three, with the reason. Use it critically. A paper mill with deep farm forestry links and its own fibre has a weaker supplier spoke than the average. A packaging converter serving one or two giant FMCG customers might have a stronger buyer spoke than the panel brands it is grouped with. Redraw the shape for the company in front of you.

The so-what line below states the conclusion the shapes draw: the branded panel and laminate makers keep the most profit because carpenters ask for the brand, while paper mills keep the least because imports set the price.

c10.story:
Results calls in this industry swing between paper-machine engineering and dealer-network marketing. Eight numbers cut through both.

Realisation per tonne for paper, or per sheet for panels, tells you about pricing power. For paper it is a direct read on the import pressure; for panels, a read on whether the brand is holding price or discounting. EBITDA margin tells you how much of the spread survives the wood bill, and the benchmark is different for each product: paper, plywood, MDF and laminates all have their own healthy range. Gross margin, wood and pulp cost against price, is the purest read on the spread; and if it is falling while volumes rise, that is a price war, not growth.

Capacity utilisation, especially on MDF, is the number that will tell you when the panel price war ends. New lines need to run above a certain level before discounting stops. Sales volume growth tells you about market share and underlying demand; a brand growing faster than the market is taking share from the unorganised sector.

Receivable days are a stress test for panel brands, which give dealers credit. If dealers are slow to pay, either demand is weak or the brand is stuffing the channel to hit targets. Capex to depreciation tells you whether a new build is underway: near one after a build means the company is coasting while lines fill, well above one means a new build is in progress. And return on capital employed is the verdict on whether all those mills and lines earn their keep through a full cycle.
c10.read:
The table has one row per number. Read across: what it tells you, what good looks like and today's industry median.

  • What it tells you is the question to ask. For this industry the questions split into three: price (realisation, gross margin), profitability and filling (EBITDA margin, utilisation, volume), and discipline (receivables, capex, ROCE).
  • What good looks like carries the benchmark, and it is the only column with figures. Note that several rows give separate marks per product: the EBITDA margin row lists paper, plywood, MDF and laminates separately, and the ROCE row separates brands from paper. Always compare a company against its own product's mark.
  • Today's industry median is drawn from the latest filings of listed companies in our database. Realisation and MDF utilisation have no median, because they come from company presentations rather than standard accounts.

A caution specific to this bucket: the listed group includes the misfiled names from door four, steel pipes, yarn and recycling, so the median is a blend. Treat it as a rough backdrop and lean more on the good mark and on peers within the same door.

The best use of the table is a three-way comparison for each company: its own number, the industry median and the good mark. For a panel maker today, the two numbers to put side by side are MDF utilisation and gross margin. If utilisation is rising and gross margin has stopped falling, the price war is ending.

c11.story:
The early warnings for paper and panels come from the edges of the industry: an import price quote, a farm-gate wood price in Andhra, a housing possession schedule, a DGTR docket.

The fastest signal is a DGTR investigation or duty on paper: if a duty lands, paper prices rise the same day. Most of the rest speak about a quarter ahead. Imported paper and pulp prices set Indian paper realisations a quarter later. Wood bought from farmers today is next quarter's production cost. FMCG volume growth becomes carton orders next quarter. Rising paper import volumes warn of price pressure ahead. The furthest-reaching signal is housing completions and possession data: homes handed over now become panel and laminate orders over the following months, about two quarters out.

Fold the signals into one rule. The industry is in an up-cycle when import prices are rising, wood costs are easing and capacity is filling. Two out of three is early recovery; one out of three is a false dawn.

Today the count is two: wood is off its peak and MDF lines are ramping. The missing sign is import prices, still low with imports heavy. And notice who benefits from the two ticks: both mainly help panels. Easing wood helps everyone, but filling MDF lines is a panel story. The missing tick, import prices, is the one paper mills need. That is why the clock reads bottoming and the call prefers branded panels and laminates over paper mills.

Two ticks out of three, but both are panel ticks. Paper is still waiting for its own.
c11.read:
The chart places each outside signal along a line by how far ahead it speaks. The further right a dot, the earlier the warning. Hover a dot to read the channel.

  • Same quarter: DGTR investigations on paper. A duty decision moves prices on the day.
  • One quarter ahead: imported paper and pulp prices, farm wood prices in Andhra and Gujarat, FMCG volume growth, and paper import volumes. This is the crowded middle of the chart, where most of a quarter is decided in advance.
  • Two quarters ahead: housing completions and possession data. The earliest warning on the chart, and the one that matters most for panel makers.

Use the chart as a reading order: start with the right-hand dot, check the middle cluster, then confirm with the left. For a panel investor, rising completions plus easing wood is the combination to look for. For a paper investor, rising import prices plus falling import volumes is the one.

Below the chart is the rule with its three signs. A tick means the sign is on, a cross means it is off, and the note gives today's state. Import prices rising: a cross, still low with imports heavy. Wood costs easing: a tick, off the peak. Capacity filling: a tick, MDF lines ramping.

The call box gives the directional view, the points behind it, and what would change it: a safeguard or anti-dumping duty on paper imports, a sharp wood price rise as farmers switch crops, or a housing slowdown that cuts interior demand. The first would be good news for paper; the other two bad news for everyone. Keep all three on your alert list.
